main.title: Rocket: Robot on Wheels
main.subtitle: Sucker Punch Productions · Nintendo 64
main.summary: Rocket: Robot on Wheels is Sucker Punch Productions' Nintendo 64 platformer about a maintenance robot rescuing a theme park from sabotage. Rocket searches for stolen tickets and tokens while pursuing Jojo, a raccoon who has taken the park's walrus mascot. The themed areas contain rides, vehicles and objects that can be manipulated to solve problems. Rather than rely only on jumping between platforms, the player has to consider how things move and interact, giving a playful mechanical purpose to the robot's work inside the park.

cards.heading: Repair the amusement park before opening
cards.text: Rocket: Robot on Wheels is Sucker Punch Productions' Nintendo 64 platformer about a maintenance robot rescuing a theme park from sabotage. Rocket searches for stolen tickets and tokens while pursuing Jojo, a raccoon who has taken the park's walrus mascot. The themed areas contain rides, vehicles and objects that can be manipulated to solve problems. Rather than rely only on jumping between platforms, the player has to consider how things move and interact, giving a playful mechanical purpose to the robot's work inside the park.

cards.heading: The object has weight and momentum
cards.text: Physics gives movable objects behaviour that needs to be understood before a puzzle can be solved reliably. Mass, friction and inertia make the result depend on how something is handled as well as where it is placed. Each area supplies a vehicle and a collection of tasks, with tickets opening further worlds and tokens purchasing abilities. A ride or machine can become another route to a reward. The player learns the park by using its attractions and discovering what a familiar object can do in a different arrangement.

cards.heading: The first game from Sucker Punch
cards.text: The studio developed a prototype before securing Nintendo development hardware and spent much of the project looking for a publisher. Ubisoft eventually released the finished game in 1999. Julian Soule composed its music. The amusement-park setting helps explain the mixture of physical experiments, vehicles and platforming routes: each area can introduce another contraption without leaving the same larger place. Rocket's role as a maintenance machine makes manipulating those systems feel like part of the character's work, with recovering the park providing a reason to keep experimenting.

main.title: Chrono Cross
main.summary: Chrono Cross is a 1999 role-playing video game developed and published by Square for the PlayStation video game console.

cards.heading: A PlayStation return to Chrono's world
cards.text: Chrono Cross is a 1999 role-playing video game developed and published by Square for the PlayStation video game console. It is set in the same world as Chrono Trigger, which was released in 1995 for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System. Chrono Cross was designed primarily by scenarist and director Masato Kato, who had help from other designers who also worked on Chrono Trigger, including art director Yasuyuki Honne and composer Yasunori Mitsuda. Nobuteru Yūki designed the characters of the game.

cards.heading: Serge faces a world where he died
cards.text: The story of Chrono Cross focuses on a teenage boy named Serge and a theme of parallel worlds. Faced with an alternate reality in which he died as a child, Serge endeavors to discover the truth of the two worlds' divergence. The flashy thief Kid and many other characters assist him in his travels around the tropical archipelago El Nido. Struggling to uncover his past and find the mysterious Frozen Flame, Serge is chiefly challenged by Lynx, a shadowy antagonist working to apprehend him.

cards.heading: Acclaim and The Radical Dreamers Edition
cards.text: Upon its release in Japan in 1999 and North America in 2000, Chrono Cross received widespread acclaim, earning a perfect 10.0 score from GameSpot. The game shipped 1.5 million copies worldwide by 2003, leading to a Greatest Hits re-release and continued life in Japan as part of the Ultimate Hits series. Chrono Cross was later re-released for the PlayStation Network in Japan in July 2011, and in North America four months later. A remaster of the game, titled Chrono Cross: The Radical Dreamers Edition was released on April 7, 2022, for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, Windows, and Xbox One.

main.title: Pokémon Gold and Silver
main.summary: Pokémon Gold Version and Pokémon Silver Version are 1999 role-playing video games developed by Game Freak and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy Color.

cards.text: Pokémon Gold Version and Pokémon Silver Version are 1999 role-playing video games developed by Game Freak and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy Color. They are the first installments in the second generation of the Pokémon video game series. They were released in Japan on November 21st, 1999, Australia and North America on October 15th, 2000, and Europe on April 6th, 2001.

The games introduce 100 new species of Pokémon and follow the progress of the player character in their quest to master Pokémon battling. Both games are independent of each other but feature largely the same plot and, while both can be played separately, it is necessary to trade between these games and their predecessors in order to fully complete each game's Pokédex. The Johto Saga of the Pokémon anime is based on the new region introduced in the games.

Pokémon Gold and Silver were both critical and commercial successes; the games sold over 23 million units, making them the best-selling games for the Game Boy Color and the third-best-selling for the Game Boy family of systems. In retrospect, they are both cited as some of the most significant titles of the fifth generation of video games, two of the best entries in the series, if not the best, and both are touted as being amongst the greatest video games of all time. The two releases are also noted to have continued the success of the Pokémon series as it began to form into a billion-dollar franchise.

A third game in the generation, Pokémon Crystal, was released in 2000. In 2009, on the 10th anniversary of Gold and Silver, remakes titled Pokémon HeartGold and SoulSilver were released for the Nintendo DS.

main.title: Donkey Kong 64
main.summary: Donkey Kong 64 is a 1999 platform game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.

cards.text: Donkey Kong 64 is a 1999 platform game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. It is the first Donkey Kong game to feature 3D gameplay. As the gorilla Donkey Kong, the player explores themed levels to collect items and rescue his family members from the crocodile King K. Rool. The player completes minigames and puzzles as five playable Kong characters—each with their own special abilities—to receive bananas and other collectibles. In multiplayer modes, up to four players can compete in deathmatch and last man standing games.

Rare began working on Donkey Kong 64 in 1997, following the completion of Donkey Kong Country 3 (1996). A 16-member team, with many staff from Rare's Banjo-Kazooie (1998) team, developed it over three years. It was conceived as a 2.5D platformer similar to Country before it was reworked into a more open-ended game using the Banjo engine. Rare sought to differentiate Donkey Kong 64 from Banjo with more collectibles and player characters, cinematic sequences, and bombastic bosses. It was the first of two games to require the Nintendo 64 Expansion Pak, an accessory that added memory resources. Grant Kirkhope composed the soundtrack, which includes a comedy hip-hop song, the "DK Rap", that plays in the introduction.

Donkey Kong 64 was released in North America in November 1999 and worldwide in December. Nintendo backed the release with a US$22 million marketing campaign that included advertisements, sweepstakes, and a national tour. Donkey Kong 64 received acclaim and was Nintendo's bestseller during the 1999 holiday season, selling 5.27 million copies worldwide by 2021. It won the 1999 E3 Game Critics award for Best Platform Game and multiple awards and nominations from magazines. Reviewers praised its visuals, size, and length, but criticized its camera and emphasis on item collection and backtracking. Some cited its gameplay and visual similarities to Banjo-Kazooie as a detriment.

Donkey Kong 64 was Rare's final Donkey Kong game before its acquisition by Microsoft in 2002, the last major Donkey Kong game until Donkey Kong Jungle Beat (2004), and the franchise's only 3D platformer until Donkey Kong Bananza (2025). Nintendo rereleased it via the Wii U's Virtual Console in 2015 and the Nintendo Classics service in 2026. Retrospective reviews were mixed; some critics considered it emblematic of the tedium in Rare's "collect-a-thon" adventure platformers for its excessive emphasis on collecting items and have blamed it for precipitating 3D platforming's decline in popularity. Video game journalists have called the "DK Rap" one of the worst songs in a video game, and it has garnered popularity as an internet meme.

main.title: Unreal Tournament
main.summary: Unreal Tournament is a 1999 first-person shooter game developed by Epic Games and Digital Extremes.

cards.text: Unreal Tournament is a 1999 first-person shooter game developed by Epic Games and Digital Extremes. The second installment in the Unreal series, it was first published by GT Interactive in 1999 for Windows, and later released on the PlayStation 2 and Dreamcast by Infogrames in 2000 and 2001, respectively. Players compete in a series of matches of various types, with the general aim of out-killing opponents. The PC and Dreamcast versions support multiplayer online or over a local area network. Free expansion packs were released, some of which were bundled with a 2000 re-release: Unreal Tournament: Game of the Year Edition.

Powered by the Unreal Engine, Unreal Tournament received universal acclaim, often being considered one of the greatest video games ever made, with reviewers praising the graphics, level design and gameplay, though the console ports were noted for having limitations. The design of the game shifted the series' focus to competitive multiplayer action with the releases of sequels Unreal Tournament 2003 in 2002, Unreal Tournament 2004 in 2004, and Unreal Tournament 3 in 2007.

In 2014, a pre-alpha version of a new game in the series was released titled simply Unreal Tournament, with the source code being freely available, but in 2017 Epic Games ceased development on it after they reallocated its development team to Fortnite Battle Royale, and a formal announcement of the end of its development was made later in December 2018.

main.title: Garou: Mark of the Wolves
main.summary: Garou: Mark of the Wolves is a 1999 fighting game developed and published by SNK for the Neo Geo arcade and home platforms.

cards.heading: A new generation enters South Town
cards.text: Garou: Mark of the Wolves is SNK's 1999 Neo Geo fighting game and the sixth main Fatal Fury entry. Ten years after Terry Bogard defeated Geese Howard, Terry and his adopted son Rock enter a new South Town tournament. Most of the fourteen fighters are new. Before a bout, the player chooses a section of the life bar for T.O.P., which grants stronger attacks while health lies within it. Just Defend adds another calculated risk: blocking at the precise moment provides advantages, making timing important even when resisting an attack.

cards.heading: Reworking Fatal Fury for newcomers
cards.text: The game was designed as an overhaul of the Fatal Fury series, as event planner Yasuyuki Oda found the franchise outdated when compared with SNK's IP, The King of Fighters. In order to reboot the series, a new protagonist, Rock Howard, was created, serving as the basis for Terry's redesign and the rest of the 12 characters, two of which are also bosses. Yasuyuki Oda and Nobuyuki Kuroki served as the main illustrators and character designers. The fighting system was created to be accessible to newcomers. The game was ported to several consoles, with the Xbox 360 port being given an online mode, whereas more modern ports aimed to give improved netcode.

cards.heading: A following that carries into another sequel
cards.text: Garou: Mark of the Wolves became one of SNK's most famous fighting games of all time for its new fighting engine and new cast, which appealed to both newcomers and returning players. Often compared with Capcom's acclaimed Street Fighter III due to the new cast and visuals, the game has frequently appeared in lists of SNK's best fighting games. Ending in a cliffhanger, the game's narrative was briefly explored in KOF: Maximum Impact among other KOF games, though no plans for sequels were conceived after two years of development. Eventually, the sequel Fatal Fury: City of the Wolves was released on April 24, 2025.

main.title: The Legend of Dragoon
main.subtitle: A rhythm inside the turn
main.summary: Japan Studio gives its four-disc fantasy an unusually physical pulse: choosing an attack is only the beginning.

cards.heading: The timing of a sword
cards.text: Released for PlayStation in Japan on December 2, 1999, The Legend of Dragoon follows Dart and companions who inherit the power of dragons. Its turn-based battles demand more than selecting commands: timed button presses extend an attack through the Addition system. Transforming into a Dragoon changes the available powers and the rhythm of combat.

cards.heading: An ambition measured in discs
cards.text: Producer Shuhei Yoshida recalled a project begun in 1996 that eventually involved more than a hundred internal developers. Pre-rendered locations and cinematic sequences filled four CDs. The team adjusted the balance after the Japanese release before bringing the game to North America in June 2000.

cards.heading: A voice beyond the battlefield
cards.text: Dennis Martin and Takeo Miratsu composed the score, with Elsa Raven singing the main theme, If You Still Believe. The vocal opening and pieces such as Battle 1 and Dart's Theme give different parts of the adventure their musical character. The original PlayStation adventure later reached new players through digital editions.

main.title: Sonic the Hedgehog Pocket Adventure
main.subtitle: Sonic visits SNK’s handheld
main.summary: Sonic the Hedgehog Pocket Adventure is SNK's Sonic platform game for Neo Geo Pocket Color, first released in North America on 4 December 1999.

cards.heading: Sonic visits SNK’s handheld
cards.text: Sonic the Hedgehog Pocket Adventure is SNK's Sonic platform game for Neo Geo Pocket Color, first released in North America on 4 December 1999. It draws on the landscapes and ideas of the Mega Drive games, particularly Sonic the Hedgehog 2, but builds new stage layouts for the handheld. Running, jumping and collecting rings preserve the familiar pace. The smaller screen gives those actions another setting while the route itself supplies new places to accelerate, explore or recover from an awkward landing.

cards.heading: Familiar places with new paths
cards.text: The game borrows recognizable themes without repeating the original layouts, making familiarity useful but insufficient to predict the next obstacle. Bonus stages also recall Sonic 2. A save feature allows completed levels to be revisited, while time trials turn them into short races against an improving personal result. Another time challenge requires at least fifty rings to count, connecting speed with keeping a supply intact. These modes give a learned route several purposes, asking the player to approach the same stretch with a different priority.

cards.heading: A short race with more reasons to return
cards.text: Two linked handhelds support competitive races or a contest to collect a target number of rings, with the second player controlling Tails. Hidden puzzle pieces assemble character portraits, and completing those puzzles opens the sound test. Sega's Yuji Naka and Sonic Team supervised SNK's production. Several developers later helped form Dimps, which went on to make further handheld Sonic games. Pocket Adventure stands at that transition, showing another studio carrying the speed and structure of the console series into a distinctive portable release.

main.title: Vib-Ribbon
main.subtitle: A rabbit on a line of music
main.summary: Vib-Ribbon is NanaOn-Sha's PlayStation rhythm game, released in Japan on 9 December 1999. Vibri walks along a thin white line as music turns the route into obstacles. The drawing is deliberately spare: a rabbit, a moving path and enough shape to show the next action. Masaya Matsuura led the project after plans for a car advertisement changed into a standalone game. Rather than fill the screen with scenery, it makes the movement of a line carry both the landscape and the rhythm the player needs to follow.

cards.heading: A rabbit on a line of music
cards.text: Vib-Ribbon is NanaOn-Sha's PlayStation rhythm game, released in Japan on 9 December 1999. Vibri walks along a thin white line as music turns the route into obstacles. The drawing is deliberately spare: a rabbit, a moving path and enough shape to show the next action. Masaya Matsuura led the project after plans for a car advertisement changed into a standalone game. Rather than fill the screen with scenery, it makes the movement of a line carry both the landscape and the rhythm the player needs to follow.

cards.heading: Four shapes, then combinations
cards.text: Blocks, loops, waves and pits correspond to four different button inputs. Pressing at the right moment lets Vibri cross each shape; combined obstacles require both responses together. Repeated mistakes transform the rabbit into a frog and then an insect, while successful play can restore her or produce the higher-scoring Super Vibri form. Damage is therefore visible in the character rather than only in a separate meter. The route remains simple to describe, but reading joined shapes and responding to the music gives the small vocabulary room to become demanding.

cards.heading: Your record becomes the road
cards.text: The software loads into the PlayStation's memory, allowing the game disc to be removed and replaced with an audio CD. Vib-Ribbon then generates routes from that record's tracks. Six built-in songs provide the initial courses, with music credited to Laugh and Peace and Matsuura, but a personal collection can supply further journeys. The idea changes an ordinary household object into level material. Europe received the original in 2000; North America first received the game through PlayStation Network in 2014, extending the life of a project whose strongest feature was its openness to other music.

main.title: Planescape: Torment
main.summary: Planescape: Torment is a 1999 role-playing video game developed by Black Isle Studios and published by Interplay Entertainment for Windows.

cards.heading: An immortal wakes in Sigil
cards.text: Planescape: Torment is a 1999 role-playing video game developed by Black Isle Studios and published by Interplay Entertainment for Windows. The game takes place in locations from the multiverse of Planescape, a Dungeons & Dragons (D&D) fantasy campaign setting. The game's engine is a modified version of the Infinity Engine, which was used previously for BioWare's Baldur's Gate, an earlier D&D game set in the Forgotten Realms.

cards.heading: Recovering the Nameless One’s past
cards.text: Planescape: Torment is primarily story-driven, with combat taking a secondary role. The protagonist, known as The Nameless One, is an immortal man who forgets everything if killed. The game focuses on his journey through the city of Sigil and other planes to reclaim his memories of previous lives, and to discover why he was made immortal in the first place. Several characters in the game may join The Nameless One on his journey; most of these characters have encountered him in the past or have been influenced by his actions in some way.

cards.heading: Critical acclaim and later editions
cards.text: The game was not a commercial success, but it received critical acclaim and has since become a cult classic, claimed by video game journalists to be the best role-playing video game of 1999. It was lauded for its immersive dialogue, for the dark and relatively obscure Planescape setting, and for the protagonist's unique persona, which shirked many characteristics of traditional role-playing games. It is commonly cited as one of the greatest video games of all time. An enhanced version for modern platforms was made by Beamdog and released for Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, and iOS in April 2017 and for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, and Xbox One in October 2019.
